title: Environment-Specific API Configuration
keywords: APIs, Asynchronous Operations, and Data Handling
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Environment-Specific API Configuration in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Environment-Specific API Configuration within APIs, Asynchronous Operations, and Data Handling. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Remote data can fail, arrive late, or become stale, so data fetching needs explicit cancellation, retry, and empty-state behavior.

content_blocks.title: Environment-Specific API Configuration: Safe rendering and trust boundaries
content_blocks.alt_text: Safe rendering and trust boundaries diagram for lesson 88: Environment-Specific API Configuration. Treat strings, URLs, and client state as untrusted → Escape text; validate URLs and payloads → Enforce access and sensitive decisions on the backend
content_blocks.caption: Security flow: untrusted values are rendered safely, while the server remains responsible for authorization and sensitive decisions.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: API integration coordinates asynchronous JavaScript, HTTP requests, server data, loading/error states, and configuration across environments. This lesson focuses on Environment-Specific API Configuration. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Development and production API URLs
items.text: For Development and production API URLs, decide which code runs during build, on the server, and in the browser. Keep output deterministic during hydration, isolate state per server request, keep secrets server-only, and test the actual production build rather than relying only on the dev server.

items.title: Client-exposed versus server-only configuration
items.text: For Client-exposed versus server-only configuration, trace the path from the entry point to the root component, then identify the configuration or tool responsible for compiling and serving it. Use the official create-vue/Vite workflow for a fresh Vue 3 project and keep dependency versions reproducible.

items.title: Avoiding secrets in browser bundles
items.text: For Avoiding secrets in browser bundles, treat browser input and browser-held state as untrusted. Prefer Vue's escaped text interpolation for plain text, avoid compiling user-provided templates, and send authorization or sensitive decisions to a server that verifies them independently.

items.title: Managing API configuration across deployments
items.text: For Managing API configuration across deployments, decide which code runs during build, on the server, and in the browser. Keep output deterministic during hydration, isolate state per server request, keep secrets server-only, and test the actual production build rather than relying only on the dev server.

content_blocks.expected_output: The frontend reads the configured public API base URL; a missing value is surfaced early instead of silently sending requests to an incorrect endpoint.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Only put public configuration in VITE_ variables. Never include private API keys or server credentials in a browser bundle.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Environment-Specific API Configuration with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Vite environment variables”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.text: Remember: API integration coordinates asynchronous JavaScript, HTTP requests, server data, loading/error states, and configuration across environments. content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Environment-Specific API Configuration” that applies “Development and production API URLs”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Development and production API URLs”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
